title: Speaking practice: A Floating Egg, a Stretch Break and a Town Flood
description: Eight speaking tasks: describe a character, explain a steady speed, explain density, argue at a town meeting, persuade a teacher, retell how a character changed, explain a late project and retell a flood timeline.

stimuli.title: Describe the main character
paragraphs: Your class is reading a novel. A classmate was absent and has not met the main character yet. Here is the character card from your notebook.
Name: Nadia. Age: 12. Home: a fishing village by the sea.
Appearance: short black hair, always wears a yellow scarf.
Personality: curious and patient.
Goal: to learn how to build a boat like her uncle.
Problem: her uncle says she is too young to use his tools.

stimuli.title: Explain a steady speed
paragraphs: A bike rider travels 45 kilometers in 3 hours. She rides at the same speed the whole time. Your friend wants to know how far she will travel in 5 hours at that same speed.
Distance: 45 kilometers. Time: 3 hours. New time: 5 hours.

stimuli.title: Why the egg floated
paragraphs: In a science demonstration, a teacher puts the same fresh egg into two jars. Each jar holds 2 cups of tap water at the same temperature.
Jar 1: plain tap water. The egg sinks to the bottom.
Jar 2: tap water with 6 tablespoons of salt stirred in until it dissolves. The egg floats near the top.
Teacher's note: Density is how much mass is packed into a certain volume. An object sinks in a liquid if it is denser than the liquid. It floats if it is less dense than the liquid.

stimuli.title: Library hours or playground?
paragraphs: A town has $50,000 to spend this year on one project. At a town meeting, residents may speak for up to a minute and a half about which project the town should choose.
Proposal 1: Replace the broken swings and slides at Elm Park.
Proposal 2: Keep the library open two extra evenings each week for one year.
Survey of 140 residents: 55 chose the park, 85 chose longer library hours.
A student says: “I use the library after school for homework and the internet.” A parent says: “The swings at Elm Park are broken.”

stimuli.title: Ask for a stretch break
paragraphs: Your class has 24 students. You took a short survey: “Do you feel tired after lunch?” 18 students said yes. 6 students said no.
You want to ask your teacher for a three-minute stretch break after lunch each day. Your teacher is worried about losing class time. The class meets 5 days each week.

stimuli.title: How a runner changed
paragraphs: Your class read a story and you will retell it to a partner who was absent. Here is the story summary.

Elena was the fastest runner in her village. When a newcomer named Sofia beat her in a race, Elena stopped talking to her and sat alone at lunch. Before the next race, Elena's shoelace snapped. Sofia, who was standing beside her at the starting line, pulled a spare lace from her bag and handed it over without a word. Elena ran well, but Sofia won again. Afterward, Elena walked over and said, “Thank you. I was wrong to ignore you. Will you train with me?” By the end of the season, the two girls ran together every morning.

stimuli.title: Why is our project behind?
paragraphs: Your group's science fair model was due on Friday. Your teacher has asked your group to explain what happened.

On Monday, two members of your group were absent for two days because of illness. On Wednesday, the group found out that the magnets ordered for the model arrived broken. The store said replacements will arrive next Monday.
You are the group member who will speak to the teacher.

stimuli.title: The Millford flood: a town museum retelling
paragraphs: You are a volunteer at the museum in the small town of Millford. A visitor asks what happened during the great flood. Here is the timeline from the museum's notes.
Day 1: After three days of heavy rain, the river rises over its banks.
Day 2: The mayor rings the town bell. Families carry blankets and food to the school on the hill.
Day 3: Water covers Main Street and the market.
Day 5: The rain stops. The water slowly goes down.
Day 9: Families return home. Volunteers clean the shops and repair the bridge.
The next year: The town builds a flood wall beside the river.

items.stem: Describe Nadia to your classmate. Tell what she looks like, two personality traits, what she wants, and her problem.

checklist: I described how Nadia looks.
I named two personality traits.
I told what Nadia wants.
I told her problem.
exemplar: Includes all four required parts (appearance, traits, goal, problem).
Uses descriptive noun groups (short black hair, a yellow scarf).
Uses present tense consistently and accurately.
Connects the goal and the problem logically.
Speaks clearly and in complete sentences.

support.clue: The card has five lines. Say one idea from each line: who she is, how she looks, her traits, her goal, her problem.
support.frame: Nadia is a ___-year-old girl who lives ______. She has ______ and she always wears ______. She is ______ and ______. She wants to ______. Her problem is that ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different character): “Omar is a 10-year-old boy who lives in a city apartment. He has curly brown hair and always wears a green cap. He is funny and brave. He wants to play the drums in the school band. His problem is that his neighbors do not like loud noise.” Now describe Nadia in the same way.

items.stem: Explain to your friend, step by step, how to find how far the rider will travel in 5 hours. Say the answer and tell why your method works.

checklist: I explained how to find the distance for 1 hour.
I used that rate to find the distance for 5 hours.
I said the final answer with its unit.
I explained why the method works.
exemplar: Finds or describes the unit rate: 45 ÷ 3 = 15 kilometers per hour.
Multiplies the rate by 5 hours to reach 75 kilometers.
Explains why this works (the speed is steady, so the same distance is covered each hour).
Uses rate language (per hour, each hour, at the same speed).
Sequences the steps with connectors.

support.clue: First find how far she goes in one hour. Then ask yourself how many one-hour trips there are in 5 hours.
support.frame: First, I find how far the rider goes in ___ hour. I divide ___ by ___, which is ___. This means she travels ___ kilometers each hour. Next, I multiply ___ by ___ because ______. So she will travel ___ kilometers in 5 hours.
support.model: Mentor example (a different situation): “A machine prints 60 pages in 5 minutes at a steady speed. First, I find how many pages it prints in 1 minute. I divide 60 by 5, which is 12. This means it prints 12 pages each minute. Next, I multiply 12 by 6 because I want to know about 6 minutes. So it will print 72 pages in 6 minutes.” Now explain the bike rider in the same way.

items.stem: Explain to your science partner why the same egg sank in Jar 1 but floated in Jar 2. Use the word density and say what the salt changed.

checklist: I compared what happened in Jar 1 and Jar 2.
I used the word density correctly.
I explained what the salt changed.
I used cause-and-effect words such as because, so, and as a result.
I stated a conclusion.
exemplar: Describes both outcomes accurately (egg sinks in plain water, floats in salt water).
Explains that the dissolved salt made the water denser.
Applies the density rule: the egg is denser than plain water but less dense than the salt water.
Uses cause-and-effect connectors and academic vocabulary (dissolve, density, float, sink).
Ends with a clear conclusion that links the evidence to the idea.

support.clue: The egg did not change between the jars. Ask what did change, and use the teacher's note to connect the change to sinking or floating.
support.frame: In Jar 1, the egg ______ because ______. In Jar 2, the teacher added ______, which made the water ______. As a result, the egg ______ because it is ______ than the salt water. This shows that ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different situation): “Two spoons, one metal and one wooden, have been in the same room all day, so they have the same temperature. The metal spoon feels colder when I touch it. The metal spoon feels colder because metal moves heat away from my hand faster than wood does. As a result, my hand loses heat quickly and the spoon feels cold. This shows that how cold something feels depends on how fast it moves heat, not only on its temperature.” Now explain the egg in the same way.

facts: A fresh egg sinks in plain tap water.
A fresh egg floats in sufficiently salty water.
Dissolving salt in water makes the water denser.
An object sinks in a liquid if it is denser than the liquid and floats if it is less dense.
Metal moves heat away from skin faster than wood does, so a metal object feels colder than a wooden object at the same temperature.

items.stem: Speak at the town meeting. Say which proposal the town should fund and support your position with at least two pieces of evidence, including numbers from the survey.

checklist: I stated which proposal the town should fund.
I used numbers from the survey.
I used at least one other detail from the prompt.
I explained why my evidence supports my position.
I used a word such as however or although to answer the other side.
exemplar: States a clear position (either proposal can be well supported).
Cites survey data accurately (85 for the library, 55 for the park, out of 140).
Includes at least one additional detail (homework and internet access, or broken equipment).
Explains how the evidence supports the decision rather than only listing it.
Briefly responds to the other side using contrast language.

support.clue: Compare 85 and 55 out of 140. Then decide which other detail is strong evidence for your choice, and which detail the other side could use.
support.frame: I believe the town should fund ______ because ______. In the survey of 140 residents, ___ chose ______ and ___ chose ______. Also, ______. Although some people say ______, ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different decision): “I believe the school should buy new microscopes because science students need them. In a survey of 90 students, 60 chose microscopes and 30 chose new basketball hoops. Also, the old microscopes have cracked lenses. Although some students say sports are important, microscopes help the whole class learn.” Now state and defend your choice for the town.

items.stem: Persuade your teacher to allow a three-minute stretch break after lunch. Use the survey results, give one way it could help the class, and answer the teacher's worry about time.

checklist: I asked politely for the break.
I used the survey numbers.
I gave one way the break could help the class.
I answered the worry about time.
exemplar: Makes a polite, clear request with persuasive language.
Cites the survey accurately (18 of 24 students, or three out of four).
Gives a reasonable benefit (more energy and focus after lunch).
Responds to the time concern (three minutes a day is fifteen minutes a week) or offers a plan.
Uses a respectful tone appropriate for a teacher.

support.clue: Think of the teacher's worry first. What number can you use to show the break is small? What numbers show many students need it?
support.frame: Could we please have ______? In our survey, ___ out of ___ students said they feel ______ after lunch. A short break could help because ______. I understand you are worried about ______, but ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different request): “Could we please have music during silent reading? In our survey, 15 out of 20 students said they concentrate better with quiet music. Soft music could help because it covers hallway noise. I understand you are worried about distraction, but we could use music without words.” Now ask your teacher for the stretch break.

facts: 18 + 6 = 24 students; 18 out of 24 is 75 percent, or three fourths.

items.stem: Retell the story to your partner and explain how Elena changed from the beginning to the end. Tell what caused the change.

checklist: I retold the main events in order.
I described Elena at the beginning and at the end.
I explained what caused her to change.
I used past tense and sequence words.
I included a closing sentence about the lesson of the story.
exemplar: Retells the main events in the correct order with sequence connectors.
Contrasts Elena at the beginning (jealous, silent, alone) and at the end (grateful, friendly, training with Sofia).
Identifies the cause of the change (Sofia's kindness with the shoelace).
Maintains accurate past tense and uses precise verbs.
Concludes with a sentence about the theme (kindness can change relationships).

support.clue: Look for the moment in the story when something Sofia did surprised Elena. Compare how Elena acted before and after that moment.
support.frame: At the beginning of the story, Elena was ______ because ______. Then, ______. Because Sofia ______, Elena ______. By the end, Elena was ______. The change happened because ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different story): “At the beginning of the story, Hugo was shy because he was new at school. Then, a classmate asked him to join the drawing club. Because the classmate listened to his ideas, Hugo started to speak up. By the end, Hugo was confident. The change happened because someone made him feel welcome.” Now retell the story of Elena and explain how she changed.

items.stem: Explain to your teacher why the group is behind. Give at least two causes and what each one led to, then suggest a plan for finishing the project.

checklist: I gave at least two causes.
I told what each cause led to.
I used connecting words such as because, so, and as a result.
I suggested a plan.
exemplar: Identifies at least two causes (absences, broken magnets) and connects each to a result (work not finished, model cannot be completed).
Uses cause-and-effect connectors accurately.
Proposes a realistic plan (work on other parts, redivide tasks, ask for a new date once replacements arrive).
Maintains a polite, responsible tone.
Organizes the explanation: situation, causes, plan, request.

support.clue: List two things that went wrong. For each one, ask: what could the group not do because of it?
support.frame: Our project is behind for two reasons. First, ______, so ______. Second, ______, which meant ______. As a result, ______. To finish the project, we plan to ______. Could we please ______?
support.model: Mentor example (a different situation): “Our poster is behind for two reasons. First, the printer ran out of ink, so we could not print our photos. Second, our team captain moved to another class, which meant we had no one to organize the work. As a result, we only have half the poster ready. To finish, we plan to draw the pictures by hand. Could we please have until Tuesday?” Now explain your group's situation.

items.stem: Retell the flood in Millford to the visitor. Tell the events in order, use the day numbers, and explain what the town did to protect itself afterward.

checklist: I told the events in the correct order.
I used day numbers or time words.
I used past tense.
I told what the town did afterward and why.
exemplar: Tells the main events in the correct order using the day markers.
Uses time and sequence expressions (on Day 2, a few days later, afterward).
Uses past tense accurately throughout.
Explains the flood wall as a response to the flood.
Includes specific details (the bell, the school on the hill, the market, the bridge).

support.clue: Go down the list from Day 1 to the next year. Say one sentence for each line and add a word that shows time passing.
support.frame: First, on Day 1, ______. Then, on Day 2, ______. On Day 3, ______. Several days later, ______. After the flood, ______. Because of the flood, the town ______.
support.model: Mentor example (a different event): “First, on Monday, the school learned that its roof was leaking. Then, on Tuesday, workers set up buckets and covered the books. On Wednesday, they repaired the roof. Several days later, the library reopened. After the repair, the school checked the roof every autumn.” Now retell what happened in Millford in the same way.
